findings.claim: html-css-js-final-mcq-04: the key's feedback says 'Code after an await resumes as a task on the single main thread.' An await continuation resumes as a microtask, not a task, and the learner page teaches exactly that: html-css-js/dom-tooling-and-async/the-event-loop/artifact.html cheat sheet lists 'then, catch, await continuation | Microtask queue' and its summary says 'Promise callbacks are microtasks and timer callbacks are tasks'. The feedback contradicts the taught model on the item that assesses it. The key itself is correct (the loop holds the main thread; verified reasoning against the same page's Activity 4 and 5).
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the key feedback, e.g. 'Correct. Code after an await resumes as a microtask on the same single main thread. A long synchronous loop holds that thread, so queued clicks and typing wait until it ends.'

findings.claim: html-css-js-final-mcq-02: the key repeat(4, 1fr) is correct (Chromium 900px viewport, the item's setup with width:100% images: 1fr tracks 213px, last cell 687-900px, document scrollWidth 900; repeat(4, 225px) and repeat(4, 25%) both put the last cell at 723-948px, scrollWidth 948; 4fr gives one 900px column). It is not a two-key item: a learner who reads 25% as 25% of 900 = 225px eliminates it together with repeat(4, 225px). But the fact that makes the key right, that fr shares the space left after the gaps, is not taught: html-css-js/html-and-css/grid/artifact.html says only 'fr is a share of the leftover space after fixed tracks', its prediction uses 'no gap', and the cheat sheet defines gap only as 'space between rows and columns'; the Course Review grid activity (html-css-js-course-review/html-css-js-review-page-and-language) uses gap: 16px with 1fr but never says how they interact, and percentage track sizes appear on no page. A learner who reasons that 1fr also ignores the gaps, or that 25% means a quarter of the space after gaps, is left guessing, so the item rewards elimination rather than the taught model.
findings.recommendation: Either replace the 25% distractor with a taught form (e.g. repeat(3, 1fr), which gives three columns, or repeat(4, minmax(240px, 1fr)), which overflows), or add one sentence to the grid page saying fr shares the space left after fixed tracks and gaps, while percentage tracks ignore gaps and can overflow.

findings.claim: html-css-js-final-mcq-21: distractor B (dialog where Tab cycles inside, Escape closes and returns focus) is rejected by feedback citing 'the expected pattern' for dialogs, but no learner page mentions a dialog or modal focus containment (grep 'dialog|modal' across all learner text: no hits). Worse, html-css-js/html-and-css/accessibility-basics/artifact.html states 'Focus must never get stuck: you must be able to Tab out of every part' and the takeaway 'Tab reaches every control ... focus is visible and never trapped', so a learner can appeal B using only a learner-page sentence: in the dialog, Tab cannot leave. The page's trap definition ('Tab, Shift+Tab or Escape cannot move it out again') would reject B, but the same page also states the stricter Tab-only rule, so two options are defensible from the learner pages. The key (slider ignores keys) is correct and taught ('Every control must work from the keyboard').
findings.recommendation: Preferred: replace the dialog log entry and distractor B with a non-barrier the pages settle without conflict, e.g. log 'Save: a native button with visible text, reached by Tab and pressed with Enter' and distractor 'The Save button: it needs an aria-label to be announced' (feedback: a button's own text is its name, as the accessibility page's audit item for <button>Subscribe</button> says). Otherwise reword B's feedback to cite the taught definition ('A keyboard trap is focus that Tab, Shift+Tab and Escape all fail to move out of; here Escape leaves and returns focus, so it is not a trap'), and either drop 'expected pattern' or add a sentence on the accessibility page about modal dialogs keeping focus inside until Escape closes them. Optionally fix the page's 'Tab out of every part' wording to 'leave every part with Tab, Shift+Tab or Escape'.

findings.claim: html-css-js-final-mcq-26: distractor C feedback says the line 'throws before any request is read'. The request has already been sent by fetch(); what fails is calling .json on the returned Promise (Node 24: TypeError ... json is not a function), so no response is ever read. 'request' should be 'response'.
findings.recommendation: Change to: 'fetch returns a promise, which has no json method, so this throws a TypeError before the response can be read.'

findings.claim: html-css-js-final-mcq-22: the stem says 'the Network panel shows the server answered 200', and distractor A's feedback relies on 'The headers show a 200'. The learner page's own Network model (html-css-js/fetch-and-browser-client/fixing-cors-spring-security-config-vs-vite-dev-proxy/artifact.html, the blocked-GET row) labels that row 'GET http://localhost:8080/api/books  CORS error' with the note 'The server handled it and answered, but the response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin', and Chrome's Network status column likewise shows 'CORS error' for this case. Learners who practised on the page did not see a 200 there. The key is unaffected because the stem states the fact outright.
findings.recommendation: Reword the stem to match the taught evidence, e.g. 'though the Spring Boot log shows the GET was handled and answered 200', and change A's feedback to 'The server log shows it answered, so Spring Security allowed the request.'
